'''''Potamogeton polygonifolius''''' or '''bog pondweed''' is an [[aquatic plant]]. It is found in shallow, nutrient-poor, usually acid standing or running water, bogs, fens and occasionally ditches.

==Description==
Bog pondweed is a perennial, growing from creeping rhizomes. The stems are up to 0.7 m long, [[terete]] and unbranched.<ref name="Preston"/> The submerged leaves are long (60–160 mm) and fairly narrow (2.5–24 mm), delicate and translucent with long (14–80 mm) [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]],<ref name='Preston'/> tending to decay rather early in the season, typically once the floating leaves appear. The floating leaves are opaque, 40–105 × 15–70 mm, usually brownish or dark green in colour with a pink tint when young, with inconspicuous secondary veins.<ref name='Preston'/> There are no [[Turion (botany)|turions]].

The inflorescences are up to 42 mm long and produce numerous small greenish flowers. The fruits are 1.9–2.6 mm × 1.4–1.9 mm, larger than [[Potamogeton coloratus|''P. coloratus'']] but smaller than [[Potamogeton natans|''P. natans'']].<ref name='Preston'/>

Bog pondweed occurs both as terrestrial plants in seeps and wet moss, and as aquatic forms, and is very variable. Terrestrial forms in particular can be very difficult to identify. It is most likely to be confused with ''P. natans'' which it resembles in general habit, but can usually be distinguished by the presence of submerged leaves (these are reduced to strap-like phyllodes in ''P. natans'') and the absence of a discoloured mark at the base of the floating leaves. The submerged leaves of ''[[Potamogeton alpinus|P. alpinus]]'' can be similar, but these are sessile. Although a common plant, bog pondweed does not seem to hybridise readily with other pondweeds, though hybrids with ''P. natans'' (''P.'' × ''gessnacensis'' <small>G.Fisch.</small>), ''[[Potamogeton gramineus|P. gramineus]]'', ''P. alpinus'' (''P.'' × ''spathulatus'' <small>Schrad. ex W.D.J.Koch & Ziz</small>), [[Potamogeton berchtoldii|''P. berchtoldii'']] (''P.'' × ''rivularis'' <small>Gillot</small>) and ''[[Potamogeton pusillus|P. pusillus]]'' have been recorded.<ref name='Preston'/>

==Distribution==
''Potamogeton polygonifolius'' is mainly restricted to western Europe (Britain, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Belgium, Denmark). It is more localised in the rest of its range including Northern Iberia, Germany, mainland Italy, Sicily, southern Scandinavia, the Baltic states, the Balkans and eastern Europe.<ref name='Sweden'>Naturhistorika riksmuseet (Sweden) [http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/mono/potamogetona/potam/potapol.html Bäcknate] Potamogeton polygonifolius Pourr., [http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/mono/potamogetona/potam/potapolv.jpg northern hemisphere range map]</ref> There are outlying populations in North Africa (Morocco, Algeria), Orkney, Shetland, the Faroes and Newfoundland, and fossils have been found in Russia.<ref name='Sweden'/> The taxonomic status of populations in the Himalayas requires confirmation.<ref name='Sweden'/> A record from China was based on a misidentification of ''[[Potamogeton distinctus|P. distinctus]]''.<ref name='Guo'/>
[[File:Potamogeton polygonifolius river.jpg|thumb|Bog pondweed, ''Potamogeton polygonifolius'', in a lake outflow in North Wales.]]

==Ecology and conservation==
In Britain and Ireland, this is one of the commonest pondweeds, occurring in almost any wet or semi-wet oligotrophic and acidic habitat so long as flow is not too rapid. It may be found in lakes, slow-flowing rivers, ponds, ditches, seeps and among bog mosses (''[[Sphagnum]]''). As its name suggests, it is common in areas of blanket bog<ref name='Preston'/><ref name='Zalew'/> but may also occur in secondary habitats such as unshaded drainage ditches in bogs<ref name='Zalew'/> and forest plantations. In British rivers it typically grows with other soft-water species such as ''[[Ranunculus flammula]]'', ''[[Carex nigra]]'', ''[[Carex rostrata|C. rostrata]]'', ''Scapania undulata'' and ''[[Equisetum fluviatile]]''.<ref name='Holmes'/> In lakes it tends to occur in base-poor, oligotrophic waters with species such as ''Littorella uniflora'', ''[[Sphagnum]]'' spp., ''[[Lobelia dortmanna]]'' and ''[[Isoetes lacustris]]''<ref name=Duigan/> especially with a peaty substrate.

''Potamogeton polygonifolius'' is tolerant of acid conditions and therefore has not been affected by the widespread acidification of upland habitats in Britain. However, in very acidified pools in Holland (pH < 5), catchment liming increased the abundance of this and other threatened species.<ref name='Dorland'/> Although it shows a strong preference for soft waters,<ref name=Smolders/> bog pondweed may also occur in calcareous but low-nutrient habitats.<ref name='BRC'/> In lowland areas it is more scattered and has declined in southern and eastern England due to nutrient enrichment.<ref name='BRC'/>

In Central Europe, ''Potamogeton polygonifolius'' is threatened, and is considered endangered in Germany, Poland, Switzerland, the Czech Republic.<ref name='Zalew'/> and Luxemburg.<ref name=Coll/> However, remaining populations in this area are still strong and reproduce freely.<ref name='Zalew'/> Bog pondweed is also a Red List species in Holland.<ref name='Dorland'/>

[[File:Potamogeton polygonifolius.jpg|thumb|left]]

==Cultivation==
Bog pondweed is not in general cultivation, although it is easy to grow. Its preference for shallow water makes it very suitable for a garden pond, but it would probably be difficult to establish in high nutrient, hard water areas.
